book.title: The Power of Your Subconscious Mind
book.author: Joseph Murphy

confidence_note: The law of belief and the repeated phrase 'Be it done unto you as you believe' are central to the book (Murphy quotes Matthew). Excluded: the loop 'I cannot, so I do not try, so I fail, so I was right' written as Murphy's own text, the mention of placebo and nocebo (modern, not in a 1963 book), and the 'physiological changes' claim. Murphy's claims are belief-based, not evidence-based; the writer must keep that visible and avoid promising results. The wood-cross case appears in a secondary summary; keep it as Murphy's own claim and do not endorse it as medicine. Writer must say clearly that the book offers it as a story, not proof.
facts: Murphy returns again and again to what he calls the law of belief: what a person believes, with conviction, tends to show up in their life.
He quotes a line from Matthew, 'Be it done unto you as you believe', as the root of this idea.
He says belief is just a thought held in the mind and accepted as true.
So a person who believes they will fail is, in his view, planting that outcome, and the reverse holds too.
He says changing the belief is the starting point; he gives practical exercises with prayer and repeated affirmation to do it.
The book makes no scientific tests of the claim; it rests on his reading and on the stories he tells of his clients.

Murphy tells of a relative of his with tuberculosis whose son handed him a piece of wood and called it a healing cross; Murphy says he recovered overnight and nobody told him the truth. This is Murphy's account, with no medical evidence in the book.
scene_details: the phrase 'Be it done unto you as you believe'
a person saying 'I can't' before starting
tension: 'I can't do this' sounds like a report. Murphy says it works more like an instruction.
opening_idea: Start with the sentence Murphy keeps quoting, 'Be it done unto you as you believe', and where he took it from.

lessons.idea: A belief is a thought you have accepted as true, so it quietly decides what you try and what you leave alone.
lessons.anchor: Murphy's law of belief and its Biblical phrase.

reflect_final: Which 'I can't' or 'that won't work' have you said recently, and what would you have tried first if you had not said it?

use_cases.situation: A colleague says 'that will never work' about a new idea.
use_cases.move: Murphy says belief shapes the attempt. Ask: what would we try first if we assumed it could work?

use_cases.situation: You catch yourself saying 'I'm not a numbers person'.
use_cases.move: Rephrase it to 'I haven't learned this yet' and do one small piece today.

use_cases.situation: A friend is down on their chances for a job.
use_cases.move: Ask what they are telling themselves about the interview and whether it is the version they want.

pocket_idea: Murphy's phrase 'Be it done unto you as you believe': notice which 'I can't' you say and what it stops you trying.

conversation_variants.punchline_idea: Murphy's most repeated line is 'Be it done unto you as you believe', and he means it as an instruction, not a comfort.
conversation_variants.thirty_sec_idea: Joseph Murphy keeps coming back to one verse from Matthew: 'Be it done unto you as you believe.' He reads it as a law: a thought you hold with conviction, even 'I can't', becomes what you act on. Change the belief first, he says. The book offers faith and anecdotes, not experiments.
conversation_variants.question_idea: Which 'I can't' do you say most often?
